To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

age, knowledge of cardiovascular risk factors, body-mass-index, current smoking status and previous report of elevated BP, current diastoli BP measurement, worship service attendance, residential distance from religious organization screening site, are important predictors of screening participation.

the following factors predicted screening response: older age, higher knowledge of risk factors, greater body mass index, smoking, elevated blood pressure, greater diastolic blood pressures, greater frequency of worship attendance, and shorter residential distance from the site.

the following factors are related to participation in cardiovascular disease prevention screening programs offered at religious organizations: age, knowledge of cardiovascular risk factors, body weight, smoking status, blood pressure status, worship service attendance, distance from religious organization, and previous participation.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development, testing, and implementation of cardiovascular disease prevention strategies that are culturally and contextually appropriate for diverse populations, including African-Americans, Hispanics, Native-Americans, and Asians.
the development and evaluation of a community based health promotion program that is designed to increase awareness and knowledge of cardiovascular disease and to promote healthy behaviors.
understanding the relationship between religious organization-based health promotion and cardiovascular disease risk factor screening response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the most important predictor of participation is a person's knowledge of cardiovascular disease.
the results of the study suggest the need to consider a wide range of factors when developing programs to encourage participation in cardiovascular disease prevention programs.

those who are more educated about cardiovascular disease risk factors and who are more likely to have a higher body mass index are more likely to participate in cardiovascular disease risk screenings offered at a religious organization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
religious organizations can play a significant role in the promotion of cardiovascular disease risk reduction programs.

religious organization-based cardiovascular disease screening is feasible, acceptable, and effective in reaching a population that is at risk for cardiovascular disease and may be difficult to reach through other means.
we need to do a better job of targeting those who have the greatest risk for cardiovascular disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
religious organizations can be effective partners in community-based screening programs.
there is a need for additional work to identify ways to encourage individuals who have not participated in risk factor screenings to do so.
religious organization-based screening programs may be an efficient and effective way to reach underserved communities.
